subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF COMPTROLLER GENERAL
speechtext:
I am glad to have an opportunity to contribute to the debate on this bill that will introduce a new member to the government bureaucracy, namely, the Comptroller General. All hon. members have heard the story that a drowning man sees his life pass before him as he is going down for the third time. The government is going through that experience right now. They are about ready to meet their Maker, and seeing their whole life passing before them, they are engaging in a little bit of deathbed repentance. That is better than no repentance at all, but I wonder just how genuine the repentance is if it comes at the last minute. It is like the boy who when he was falling over a cliff said "Lord save me"; and just then his clothes caught on a branch, whereupon he said "Never mind, Lord, the tree has got me". That is the way the government feels about repentance.
The provision for a comptroller general is a kind of commentary on the government itself. While we on this side called for the creation of this office in the government, I do find two very serious shortcomings in the way the government has brought this bill forward. First of all, it has nothing to do with the establishing of the levels of the budget, and the government can tax all it wants in spite of the creation of this new office. It can continue to tax the Canadian people, and the comptroller general has no control over that. If the government has any kind of self-control or sense of feeling for the Canadian people and the weight of the burden they are already carrying in taxation, there would be no need for the office of comptroller general.
What we need is a little historical sketch as to where we have come in the institution of parliament. Many centuries ago

it was the king who had the ultimate, total and absolute control over the powers of taxation and spending. He could act according to his whims, and it was not until the barons got hold of him at a place called Runnymede, England that they began to limit the exercise of his powers. Some time after that the House of Commons began to limit the powers of the king and say, "Look, you are going to have to come to us before you can exercise those so-called unlimited powers." Parliament then began to limit the taxation powers of the king.
Today, we have the emperor opposite, as he has been described tonight by the member for York-Simcoe, who feels that it is his prerogative to tax the Canadian people as much as he wants, and it is the prerogative of the Canadian people to pay without murmuring. That is noblesse oblige to do that. Over the centuries parliament began to control the taxation and spending powers of the king, but in one fell swoop over the past ten years the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been able to undo all the progress that the House of Commons was able to establish over the centuries.
We now face a government headed by a Prime Minister who feels that the only limits that ought to be exercised are the limits of endurance of the Canadian taxpayers and that they ought not to squeal. The government's principle is to tax as much as possible rather than as little as possible. Having taxed as much as possible, it is then the responsibility of the government to spend as much as possible rather than as little as possible.
I noted with interest that Pat Carney, one of our economists in British Columbia and now one of our candidates in Vancouver Centre-and who is going to turf out that Liberal who wants to make it-has said that the country is facing a potential taxpayers' revolt. I can understand that. The one who wants to be the Liberal candidate, the former mayor of Vancouver, illustrated Liberal economics very well in the way he is going for the nomination. As Pat Carney pointed out in her speech, he bought ads for $1,900 in major Vancouver newspapers which go all over the province-and obviously most of the readers are not eligible to vote for the man in Vancouver Centre-to get himself nominated in Vancouver Centre. That is the way the Liberals look at things.
I read an article in the Globe and Mail this morning about what one of the government backbenchers is experiencing in the city of Toronto, and that article said:
But, according to one senior Metro-area Liberal MP who has spent the past three week ends knocking on doors in his suburban riding, he doesn't need a public opinion poll to tell him that "it's turned to jelly in the past two months."
That is, the decline in support for the Liberal government.
The decline in Liberal support in his riding is palpable, he told a reporter over lunch, and he wasn't the least surprised that Mr. Trudeau and his advisers are attempting to get another reading of the lie of the land.
His constituents are expressing a general feeling of irritation and concern, a lack of confidence in the way things are going in the country and in their economic prospects, he said. This is, coupled with an increased antagonism toward Mr. Trudeau.
To his surprise, this feeling includes an element of distrust, and when he probed for the reasons, Mr. Trudeau's flip-flop on the issue of wage and price controls was often cited.
May 1, 1978

The problem that we are facing in this country is that the government feels it can do anything it wants; it can make any promises it wants, and it does not have to deliver those promises if it does not want to. The taxpayers of Canada, as 1 have said, are going to revolt and change all of that as soon as the Prime Minister screws up his nerve. There has to be a limit to taxation and spending in our country.
As constituted in this legislation, the office of comptroller general really does not deal with the issue of the level of increase in the budget. In the past few days the papers have been reporting the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is raising another $700 million in West Germany by a bond issue. Canadians are concerned about the interest that it is going to cost us in addition to the 12 per cent or 15 per cent that we are going to have to pay in exchange rates on that loan. The bill does not provide any kind of priorities in the way the budget is established.
A few months ago I went to visit a constituent of mine in Crescent Beach. I went to his office, and I spoke to his wife who was running the office because the gentleman cannot work any more. He is a veteran of World War II who was captured by the Japanese and held in a prisoner of war camp in the South Pacific. Many of the prisoners of war in those South Pacific camps suffered from malnutrition. When he came home he was emaciated, but after a little fattening up he looked all right, so veterans affairs discharged him.
Now, 30 years later, he is suffering from ancillary diseases resulting from his malnutrition during the war years, and he would like to get a disability pension. However, the government have an austerity program in operation and they just cannot afford the extra dollars that it would cost to give this man the kind of disability pension that he deserves. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) says that these men will understand very well because they are good Canadians; they will understand that we are on an austerity program and the government just does not have the money.
All the understanding in the world, regardless of how good these men are as Canadians, does not fill their stomachs. They still need that money to live on. Think of that, Mr. Speaker, and then think of the fact, as has been outlined in newspaper reports brought to the attention of the House last week, that the government has every intention of paying the $10,000 fine that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) incurred as a result of slandering one of his civil servants. The government is not only going to pay the fine but also the legal fees to appeal the decision. There seems to be all kinds of money for that but somehow there is not enough to pay those veterans who suffered in a prisoner of war camp and who would like to have another $150 or $200 per month-and deserve it.
Somehow our priorities are all mixed up, Mr. Speaker. Those who are able bodied-I will keep it at able bodied when I speak of the Minister of Supply and Services because I do not know if there is any ability in any other direction-but able bodied people like the minister get all the attention while
Financial Administration Act
a man who is totally disadvantaged, whose wife now has to run the business because he cannot, does not get the attention he deserves.
This bill, which brings into being another officer who supposedly controls spending, does nothing about the priorities the government is establishing. What happened to the austerity the Minister of Veterans Affairs spoke of? Where did this $10,000 come from all of a sudden? Maybe the government could print it. As I have said before, the United States has Fort Knox and Canada has the Reid Paper Company. That is just about the way we get our extra money. I think the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) was quite right when he said last week that the government pays the expenses which accrue to a minister in the line of his duty. Now it has obviously decided that slandering one of his public servants is in a minister's line of duty and so the government is going to pay the expenses.
This bill holds out the possibility-and only the possibility- that the comptroller general will have some influence in controlling spending within the already established priorities. The second major shortcoming I see in the bill is that the comptroller general will have no effective control over spending. It is a short bill, Mr. Speaker, only one paragraph, and that is one of the delightful things about it. I wish there was more legislation like that.
For an understanding of Bill C-10 we must refer to the speech made by the minister in this House on March 8 on second reading. Obviously if the minister made a speech in the House it is recorded in Hansard. Nevertheless, he took the trouble to have it copied and sent to each member of the House. I do not know why he had to go to that expense when we could have read it in Hansard. Referring to the position of the comptroller general, the second paragraph of his speech notes:
... will be responsible to the Treasury Board for the quality and integrity of financial administrative systems and related practices and prcedures ...
You will note that he is responsible to the President of the Treasury Board, Mr. Speaker. Surely if the government is serious about controlling spending it would not mind if the comptroller general were responsible to the House of Commons or the public accounts committee. If they were serious about wanting an examination of how well they have lived within their means, they would not mind that; but perhaps the minister is a little bit nervous about letting the House of Commons look at the comptroller general's report before it has been dealt with by Treasury Board.
The next paragraph states:
Since the comptroller general will report to the President of the Treasury Board and will represent a new and somewhat specialized organization serving the Treasury Board,...
Mr. Speaker, we do not need someone else serving the Treasury Board. What we need is a tyrant-someone who will ride herd on the Treasury Board, someone who will sensitize their conscience. We do not need a servant of the Treasury Board. The next paragraph reads as follows:

May 1, 1978
Financial Administration Act
In my previous statement, Mr. Speaker, I outlined the main duties and responsibilities of this new position. As well as responsibility to the Treasury Board for the quality and integrity of the financial administrative policies, practices, and control systems, the comptroller general will also develop and maintain policies, procedures and practices necessary to evaluate and report upon the efficiency and effectiveness of government programs.
That sounds good, Mr. Speaker, but if you look at the premise upon which it is based it is that he is responsible to the Treasury Board for all his actions and reporting.
On page 2 of his speech we come across this statement:
... as the legislation before the House clearly indicates, the comptroller general would report to the government through the President of the Treasury Board.
Why not report to parliament? Why not to the House of Commons-to the public accounts committee? There it would get detailed examination and scrutiny. The sentence that really disturbs me, however, is this one:
The systems that will fall within the comptroller general's purview are intended to ensure that the government has timely, accurate and comprehensive information.
Is it to be his job to collect information and give it to Treasury Board? It seems to me that in business practice the job of a comptroller general is to stop spending, not simply to provide information-to say "You have gone as far as you can, go no further."
From the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board it looks as though it is his intention that the Comptroller General will simply provide information to the government, not stop it spending as it should be stopped.
One page 3 of his speech the minister says:
I want to reiterate that the introduction of this new office will not in any way change the responsibility of the secretary of the Treasury Board in the field of resource allocation.
There is nothing about priorities in this bill, Mr. Speaker. The comptroller general is not going to be able to tell a minister that he will get 3 per cent, 5 per cent or 7 per cent but no more. It is still up to the President of the Treasury Board and the other ministers to decide how much they are going to spend.
As the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) pointed out several times in this House, a pattern is developing in departments such as DREE, external affairs, secretary of state; we see a ballooning of their administrative expenses. This, of course, leaves less money to be used for the purposes for which the funds were intended originally.
The minister went on to say:
As I explained in detail to the Public Accounts Committee last April 26, the secretary will retain responsibility for the direction of the resource allocation and the control processes of funds; and ensure that they will not be reallocated without due authority.
So there will not be a recycling of funds. I welcome the limitation to be put on government in this respect so that unused funds cannot be put back into consolidated revenue or some other department. There will possibly be closer scrutiny of those one dollar items in the blue book.
Those are the two main concerns I have about the legislation, Mr. Speaker. There is no assurance that it is going to stop

or curtail government expenditure in any serious way. It has nothing to do with the establishment of the levels of the budget and the amount of spending. It simply says that when the Cabinet establishes spending limits the Comptroller General will make sure that they stay within those limits. That is some kind of help. But as long as it is the cabinet which sets those limits, the needs of the Canadian people will not be met.
It appears to me from what the minister has said that there will be no real power in the office of the Comptroller General such as to seriously limit government spending. Therefore, while this is the best that we can get out of the legislation, to that extent I suppose we must support it. It is far short of what we in the opposition had in mind when we suggested that the government create this office so that there would be genuine control of government spending.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF COMPTROLLER GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to speak on third reading of this debate. This matter has taken up a great deal of my time and concern since its first introduction into the House. While this debate is coming to a close, I think it is worth-while to remind the House and the country of the reasons for this piece of legislation and how it came about.
The House will recollect-and I hope the country will recollect and not forget-the Auditor General's report of 1975 in which he stated, and I quote:
The present state of the financial management and control systems of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
This is the kind of audit which, if contained in the annual statement of a privately held corporation or a corporation trading on the public stock exchange, would result in the delisting of that stock by the provincial securities commission. It would certainly result in a fall in the value of that stock and it would result in any decent, self-respecting investment broker or banker ceasing to have anything to do with a business that received an audit like that.
There was a recommendation attached to that statement of the quality of the comptroller. It stated that a comptroller general, a chief financial officer, be established to monitor the control systems of government so that these types of criticisms would not be applicable in the future. The government's response to that was exemplified by testimony before the public accounts committee. I quote from page 18:3 where the then secretary of the Treasury Board was asked this question by a Liberal member of that public accounts committee, the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson):
Do you not feel there should be a chief financial officer?
To which the then secretary of Treasury Board, Mr. Osbaldes-ton, replied:
No, sir, I believe a government governs and the government is responsible for doing so and is accountable to the country and it must discharge that responsibility. I say that very directly.
May 1, 1978

That was the initial response of the government. It said no, that its job was to govern. It is responsible to the people, and regardless of what the Auditor General says or recommends the government intends to ignore it.
In the 1976 report of the Auditor General, a year later, after further examination the Auditor General was moved to say: Based on the study of the systems of departments, agencies and Crown Corporations audited by the Auditor General financial management and control in the Government of Canada is grossly inadequate. Furthermore it is likely to remain so until the government takes strong, appropriate and effective measures to rectify this critically serious situation.
I cannot comprehend any publicly held company remaining in business if it received an audit such as that. It would surely be driven out of business. Finally, after being told in such harsh terms as an auditor could possibly use, the government started to concede a little bit and said that they might consider the recommendation of the Auditor General and establish the office of a comptroller general. On April 25, 1977 the new President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras)-the former president of the Treasury Board who refused to accept this recommendation in the first place is the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien)-said that the government had decided to go along with the recommendation and establish the position of a comptroller general.
The government said that this comptroller general would have a special functional relationship with the chief financial officers, departments and agencies, but he went on to make it clear that the ongoing responsibilities of the secretary of Treasury Board would remain the same. In other words, he made it clear there would not be much change. He ended his statement with a bit of flimflammery of the type the President of the Treasury Board likes to use, namely, "we are endeavouring to give further evidence of our determination to maintain the highest standards of control." What an absurd statement, Mr. Speaker. The Auditor General said that the control standards were grossly inadequate. The President of the Treasury Board said that they will continue to maintain the highest standards of control. That is more flimflammery.
What is the responsibility of Treasury Board in regard to financial management control? The Financial Administration Act states that the Treasury Board has the responsibility for financial management, including estimates, expenditures, financial commitments, accounts, fees, or charges for the provision of services or the use of facilities, rentals, licences, leases, revenues from the disposition of property, and procedures by which departments manage, record and account for revenues received or receivable from any source whatever.
In other words, according to the Financial Administration Act, Treasury Board already has responsibility for the financial management and control of its departments and agencies, a responsibility which it has totally failed to uphold. For the President of the Treasury Board to say "we will maintain those standards" I say is absurd.
After the denial and dismissal of the Auditor General's recommendation of a comptroller general and the subsequent admission that maybe the Auditor General's recommendation
Financial Administration Act
had some merit, what do we get? We get a one-line bill which says there shall be created another deputy minister. That is all that the bill says. It is true that the deputy minister shall have a fancy name, that his name shall be "Comptroller General." But what is in a name, after all? If a rose by any other name is a rose, then a deputy minister by any other name is a deputy minister. All this bill does is give us another deputy minister and nothing more.
The Auditor General's recommendations set out in great detail a restructuring of Treasury Board and the types of functions, responsibilities and activities that the comptroller general will engage in. These are set out in paragraph 2.15 of the Auditor General's report of 1976. I will not repeat them because they are here for everyone to see. What the Auditor General recommended was a substantial restructuring of the Treasury Board with the specific responsibilities of the comptroller general spelled out.
Why is there nothing in this act to reflect that particular recommendation of the Auditor General? When one asked the minister about this, as he was asked repeatedly in the House and in committee, he said that they operate under a system of ministerial responsibility. He said ministers are responsible to the House for what their deputies do. In no way whatsoever. The government holds constantly to this principle of ministerial responsibility when it would deny the House of Commons access to information or deny it the right to take any initiative with regard to certain legislation. But when it comes to admitting that it has failed to exercise proper supervision over the expenditure of taxpayers' money, it is quite another story. Do we ever hear of ministers resigning in such circumstances? Not on your life.
What are the chances of success for the comptroller general? We on this side hope he is outstandingly successful, but if I were a betting man I would bet that his chances of success are next to nil. What are we giving him by way of authority to move into government and cure the ills which the Auditor General describes as horrendous? He will walk into an operation which has carried the responsibility all along; he will walk into a Treasury Board structure which has proved to be a total failure, without any legislative authority; in short, it is without any tools with which to accomplish the job.
He will, it is true, be given a set of guidelines laying out a general job description. I should like to mention just one item:
Design and implementation guidance with respect to systems of financial reporting, financial management and financial control to provide assurance that public monies and assets are expended with probity, economy and efficiency and that public monies and assets are under effective custody and control. Assessment of the adequacy of such systems in departments and agencies.
The key word here is "guidance". In other words, the comptroller general will not have the authority to instal systems of financial management and control which will work. He will simply provide guidance. He will, in effect, be some kind of co-ordinator or teacher. That is no authority at all, Mr. Speaker; he will be eaten alive. Those 500,000 civil servants who have been operating out of control, according to the

May 1, 1978
Financial Administration Act
Auditor General, will continue in the future as they have in the past. We are told that the minister will give the comptroller general the necessary authority, because the minister is responsible. But will the minister live up to that responsibility? I have not seen any president of Treasury Board resigning although the president of any company who receives an auditor's report similar to the one the government received would be gone within 24 hours. The fact is that the comptroller general is going into the den of lions with no weapons whatever.
What our party tried to do in committee and on report stage was to strengthen this position. I regret that at the report stage I was not able to be here to present my motion personally; I thank my hon. friend from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for doing so on my behalf. That amendment, had it been accepted, would, it is true, not have answered all the questions I have raised but it would have given the Comptroller General a certain legislative authority; he could have approached his task in the knowledge that the House of Commons had vested him with responsibility by statute to look after such things as the form of the estimates, the effective control of public moneys and assets, making sure that financial procedures and reports conform to accepted accounting principles and that expenditures of public money are made with due regard for economy and efficiency. He could have acted to see that specific steps were taken to measure the effectiveness of government programs.
A provision of this kind in the statute would have given him some leverage so that when he met the resistance which will surely be forthcoming he would have the necessary power to overcome it. It was a simple amendment and a reasonable one. Indeed, it contained an additional sentence-"that without restricting the generality of the foregoing he should be allotted such functions as may be assigned to him by Treasury Board." Had this amendment been accepted it would have made the task of the comptroller general easy. But it was something which the government was not willing to accept. Why? Because the government has no intention of changing things in any way.
The bill before us, the appointment of this individual, is simply window dressing for the benefit of the public. The government is trying to say: "Look, we are doing something about the fact that your tax dollars are being spent in foolish, inefficient and wasteful fashion; we have appointed the comptroller general." Nonsense, Mr. Speaker. They have appointed another deputy minister, that is all, and the same old gang will carry on just as they carried on before.
That was the only amendment we put forward in committee. Another had to do with the making of an annual report to parliament, through Treasury Board, which would stand permanently referred to the appropriate committee. In that way members of parliament would at least have an opportunity to examine the report on an annual basis, to question the comptroller general and to establish where he was meeting resistance with a view to backing him up should he need support. Again, we ran into opposition. The minister claimed that in

accordance with our parliamentary traditions a committee of the House could not be involved in the manner suggested. To put it another way, it amounts to some sort of rude interference when members of parliament seek effective ways of expressing concern about the manner in which taxpayers' money is being spent. Such things, we are told, are the prerogative of members of Treasury Board. But when things are getting out of hand, don't expect the minister to resign. No way.
We also introduced in committee, unfortunately without success, a sunset clause. We agreed with the recommendation of the Auditor General that something had to be done about the fact that financial controls within government were nonexistent, but we also recognized that the course proposed might not be the answer to the problem. There is a possibility that it will not succeed. There is a possibility that costs may be too high. After all, imposing another central agency on such a huge operation like this may restrict the flexibility of the government. It may introduce inefficiencies in itself, and so we think it only wise that when we take a step like this and create a new office, a new structure and a new way of doing things, we put in a sunset clause so that five years, eight years, ten years or whatever, at some point in the future the House of Commons asks itself what it did five years ago, what it put in place at that time, whether it is working, whether it should carry on as before and whether it should be dropped, amended or changed. At some time we should look into it. To me that is the only responsible action.
However, again we ran into resistance from the government and from the minister. The minister said the government could not tolerate that kind of interference by parliament in the operations of government because, after all, parliament has no right to interfere in the operations of government; parliament should mind its own business. I have always felt that the business of parliament is government, but apparently hon. members opposite do not think so.
So it is with some degree of sadness that I see this stage of this bill nearing its completion. It is a nothing bill, really. It appoints another deputy minister, that is all, full stop. We obviously cannot be opposed to nothing, and therefore we are not opposed to this bill. But I hope the public of Canada is not deluded into believing that this piece of legislation is a response to the observations of the Auditor General with regard to the quality of financial management and control of Canada's taxpayers' money because it is not. This is a nothing bill which does nothing in terms of solving the problems articulated by the Auditor General some three years ago and which remain outstanding. Given the level of taxation in this country and the amount of money which is just wasted through inefficient practices, it is indeed a tragedy that we carry on as before and an even worse tragedy that we have such an irresponsible government.
In closing, let me repeat that we on this side wish the new Comptroller General well. According to my knowledge of his
May 1, 1978

background, he is a person of exceptional qualifications, and perhaps he will be able to overcome the obstacles which will be put in front of him. I am not optimistic in that regard. If I were a betting man, I would bet that he will fail. I am saddened that we on this side of the House were not able to give him the legislative back-up necessary so that he could get to the root of the problems and improve the quality of financial management and control within the federal government. However, until the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) screws up his courage and gives the people of Canada an opportunity to do something about it, we have to live with the recommendations of that group opposite. Hence, it is our intention to let the bill pass at third reading with the realization that the job we face when we assume office will be that much harder.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF COMPTROLLER GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his concluding remarks the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) said that this is a nothing bill, and I do not know whether the Canadian public realizes just how much nothing there is in it. The bill purports to appoint an officer called the Comptroller General of Canada to hold office during pleasure. The bill goes on to say the following, "and to perform such duties and functions as may be assigned to him by the Treasury Board". That is the extent of the bill.
The explanatory note, which generally elaborates on the intent of a bill, says much the same thing, and then it says, "and to provide for the assignment of duties and functions to the incumbent of that office". As I see it, the explanatory note is very misleading. You would be bound to agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that to provide for the assignment of duties when there is no assignment of duties here-because the wording of the bill is "and to perform such duties and functions as may be assigned to him by the Treasury Board"-is a contradiction. There is a contradiction between the text of the bill and the explanatory note which I find more than a little disturbing.
I have forgotten just how many years ago it was-perhaps two or three-but I recall the circumstances under which the concept of a comptroller general came to the fore. It stemmed basically from a remark in one of the reports of the Auditor General to the effect that the accounts of the Government of Canada were in such a deplorable state-I am paraphrasing, but this was certainly the intent of his comment-that the day might come, and come soon, when the Auditor General would be unable to certify them as being accurate. That is a very serious indictment of the accounts of any organization, but for one which has a budget of some $42 billion, all of which is raised through taxation of the Canadian population or by other means, it is a damning indictment. It is an indictment of the accounting record of this government.
In addition to that background I remember one report in which the Auditor General recommended the establishment of the position of comptroller general. I think that was in the 1976 report. At that point that government stood up and said it did not need a comptroller general at all, that it had everything in hand and that instead of appointing a comptroller general it would appoint a royal commission of inquiry on
Financial Administration Act
financial management and accountability in the Government of Canada.
The government said that a royal commission would soon satisfy all the needs and allay all the worries of the Auditor General. That was the first reaction of the government. A commission was duly appointed. It was chaired by Mr. Lambert of the board of the Toronto Dominion Bank. There vere other members including a former public servant who was at the time the deputy minister of industry, trade and commerce. Time went on. I have forgotten just how much time passed. Then all of a sudden we understand that a selection process took place and a comptroller general was named. There was some questioning and prodding: Why this change from the royal commission approach, which was supposed to solve all problems, to what appears to be an acquiescence in or an agreement with what the Auditor General said? I do not think we really know the background on that story, unless it was that the government became particularly worried. However, what concerns me is that this turnaround is a mark of indecision and evidence of a lack of good financial control over accounts, and looking at the ten-year record of this government in financial terms and in parliamentary terms, I think the Canadian people have cause for serious misgivings about the promises and undertakings which are set forth in this bill. I would like to see it otherwise.
It was suggested by my friend who spoke just before me, the hon. member for Calgary Centre, that it was just the appointment of another deputy minister, nothing more. Certainly the powers that will be given to him are not now being exercised by the Treasury Board. They may or may not be those which were outlined by the Auditor General, and I shall come to them in a few minutes because I want to talk about some of them in particular terms. As I said, with the record of this government in the matter of ministerial responsibility, we have seen time and time again when the government has developed a new theory or a new principle, and I call the principle one of ministerial abdication. The government is prepared to slough off on to the public servant responsibility for acts which are properly the government's acts. So if the comptroller general does something wrong, it is his fault and out he goes.
This has been done in the case of the public servant, Mr. Stopforth, whose name, we find, has been cleared, although the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) defamed him in public. It is not one of the ministerial responsibilities to defame a public servant, and therefore it is not the responsibility of parliament or of the Canadian people to make good the judicial judgment at a trial covering that matter. It is the individual responsibility of the minister who has defamed the public servant to do so.
So in the matter of ministerial responsibility this government has shown itself to be utterly deficient. Let me recall that this government has managed to create just this year a deficit equal to the whole budgetary spending program the year it took office-that is, $10 billion. Is that a record of monetary

May 1, 1978
Financial Administration Act
or fiscal responsibility? Yet we are expected to accept that sort of bill as an undertaking to provide what is required according to the Auditor General. And I certainly subscribe to the words of the Auditor General when he says that this sort of operation is needed. We have been asked to sign a blank cheque to allow a government with such a record to define in all secrecy- because this government is known, in addition to all its other defects, to operate in complete secrecy-the responsibilities of a comptroller general once he has been placed in office.
I ask myself: When it abdicates its responsibilities in one area, why should the government expect us to accept the notion that it will perform any more satisfactorily in another area? Its fiscal record is so abominable and so abysmal, I suggest, that we have every reason to think that in this area it will be unable to meet expectations. Therefore, we really do need a clearer definition in the legislation of the functions and responsibilities of the person whose post is being created by this legislation. We are not safe with a government with such a record of secrecy and we need an assurance in law that control will be carried out, in accordance with the efforts made by my colleagues in committee and at report stage to have the appropriate amendments brought in, efforts which were defeated by this government by sheer weight of number.
Perhaps we should ask ourselves what is a comptroller general. My first action, when I run into an expression like that, is to seek the dictionary definition as guidance. So I went to the 12 volume edition of the Oxford dictionary where I found the following definition of the word "comptroller":
An erroneous spelling of controller, introduced cl500, and formerly frequent in all senses; still retained in certain official designations, while in others it has been changed to the ordinary spelling.
So the word "comptroller" is really the erroneous spelling of the word "controller", which is more commonly used in English. I suspect it was done by a scribe who found it easier to write the word comptroller, which comes from the French word "compter", one who holds accounts. Then I went to the definition of "controller" and I found four or five definitions here. One reads:
One who keeps a counter-roll so as to check a treasurer or person in charge of accounts.
Another reads:
A household officer whose duty was primarily to check expenditure ...
Another reads:
An officer having similar duties in various public offices.
Another one is:
One who takes to task, calls in question, reproves, or censures: a censorious critic.
This is the definition which really meets the case. Another definition is:
One who controls or keeps under control; one who restrains, directs or manages.
That is what we need; we need a restrainer around here. Another definition reads:
Controller-general: an officer entrusted with the supreme direction or control.

Those are not the sorts of definitions that would be all that meaningful in an act, but surely when this act was being drafted there were some competent legal people who could define in two languages what a comptroller general was supposed to do and could put it into the bill.
I took a hint from my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary Centre, and I looked up the distinction that was made by the Auditor General when he was discussing the role of the future comptroller general. I think it is worth putting on the record again and again-it cannot be repeated too often-just what he saw the comptroller general as being required to do. These are the terms that should have gone into the bill. The Auditor General examined the structure of the Treasury Board and he said:
All functions relating to financial management and control would be assigned to the comptroller general of Canada,-
-leaving aside those of the secretary of the Treasury Board relating to resource allocation, personnel policy, administrative policy, and management of the official languages program, which would remain with the secretary of the Treasury Board or would otherwise be assigned as the government may see fit. He went on to say that the responsibilities of the comptroller general "relative to other deputy heads and his relationships with departmental financial officers are described in Part 3 of this report," to which I may have an opportunity to come.
Although this part is important, I consider it secondary this evening because my time is limited. There were five principal functions set down and I think they should be listed so that they are known. I know that in common law it is not the discussion surrounding a bill or an act which determines definitions in courts of law. For a better understanding of the meaning of this bill, the five functions of the Comptroller General should be laid down as they were seen by the Auditor General. As reported on page 3589 of Hansard, his responsibilities would be as follows:
His basic responsibilities would include the design, development, implementation and monitoring of adequate systems and procedures to ensure that the form of the estimates provides a sound basis for the government's budgetary control system,...
All of us have complained about the estimates, the difficulties which are faced when reading the estimates and extracting something from them which is meaningful. We can criticize, examine and approve, but the estimates are deemed to be approved at the end of this month if they are not passed by deliberate act.
His second responsibility would be as follows:
... that accounting procedures and financial reports throughout government... conform to acceptable accounting principles and standards .. .
In itself that is an indictment of what is now the practice, or it would not have to be said. It is a shameful thing for a public servant to feel it is necessary to advise parliament in this regard.
May 1, 1978

His third responsibility would be:
... that expenditures of public moneys are made with due regard for economy and efficiency ...
This is a most important responsibility.
The fourth one would be:
... that satisfactory procedures measure the effectiveness of programs where they could reasonably be expected to apply.
His fifth responsibility would be:
The responsibility for maintaining the central accounts of Canada would be transferred to the office of the Comptroller General from the Department of Supply and Services where it is now located.
To that I say, "Amen". Nothing should be left in the hands of the Department of Supply and Services and its minister.
I have in my possession a publication entitled, "Guide on Financial Administration for Departments and Agencies of the Government of Canada". It is signed by a previous president of the Treasury Board and is dated September, 1973. Apparently it is full of meaninglessness, and was discarded by the Auditor General. How many thousands of copies of this were produced and distributed for guidance?
Certainly we need accountability and efficiency in the economy in order for us to know if the programs undertaken by the government are meaningful. This could lead us to zero-based budgeting, whereby programs start from zero and the individuals working on those programs are required to justify what they are doing. This will not be an easy process, but it ought to be introduced early.
That zero-based budgeting, which is an effective tool of management, could be started within the departments first, and then expanded on a department by department basis. The export development program regarding the line of credit to Algeria amounted to $1.2 billion. Can that program be examined? Would it stand up under the criteria of efficiency and economy? What about the Eneraction program? I call it the enervation program. In that program, people are taken off the dole and asked to assist in the provision of insulation for the elderly. These people know nothing about insulation or construction. They have applied for a grant to operate the government program. They undertake to train people in the field of insulating houses. People are taken from the unemployment insurance rolls to be trained. These people know nothing about construction or construction standards. The result of that program is that qualified insulators are going on the unemployment rolls. They are unable to get work because of this program.
There is a great need for an examination of the economy and the efficiency of government programs. The comptroller general should be encouraging department heads to examine programs such as these. This is the area in which his relationship with other government departments would come into play. Department heads could come to him indicating that they do not know if the Eneraction program is working or not. A system of examination, assessment and evaluation could be worked out to deterthine whether returns were being paid in the form of economy and efficiency. If not, then the program
Financial Administration Act
must be dropped. I use this program merely as an example. The public will never hear about these programs unless the comptroller general is given the real power he requires to assure economy and efficiency in government operations.
Surely it is not too much to ask for these clarifications to be added to the bill. As the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) suggested, there should be an annual report to parliament from the comptroller general so that parliament would know the comptroller general was exercising his functions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF COMPTROLLER GENERAL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF COMPTROLLER GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-10. The successful passage of this very important and long-awaited piece of legislation will enable the establishment of the office of the comptroller general of Canada. The setting up of a watch dog over the spending spree of the government is long overdue.
After grim warnings from the Auditor General that the federal government has pretty well lost control of the public purse, and as a result of persistent prodding from members of my party, finally we are close to starting along the long road to introducing some economic sanity into the government and its spending. The prodigal son spending approach of the government has led this country to the brink of bankruptcy. Elected officials must register their concern and fully support this bill. It is hoped that the appointment of the comptroller general will improve financial management and introduce some degree of accountability. Similar sentiment has been expressed by the Auditor General in his annual report.
One of the basic functions of parliament is responsibility for the public purse. We in the opposition consistently have been vigilant in requiring accountability for government spending. I must confess it has been a most frustrating experience. As a member of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, I am well aware of the lack of accountability exhibited by the government. The committees have failed miserably in their efforts to apply brakes on excessive government spending. Through their long and extended testimony, ministers have tried to undermine the parliamentary tradition of scrutinizing government spending.
In its progress report of November 1977, the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability said the following:
We are persuaded that if accountability is to have full meaning and real effect, parliament must be a vital part of it.
I am one of those of the opinion that surveillance of government spending by parliamentary committees ought to be made more effective. A regular review of government departments should be conducted. We sorely lack effective mechanisms for obtaining government accountability. Accountability to parliament and to the people of Canada is the most essential element of our democratic process. If for some reason this privilege is abused, it plunges us into the kind of economic chaos we have been led into.

May 1, 1978
Financial Administration Act
Consider for the moment the following. Between 1969 and 1977 public expenditure amounted to S235 billion. The startling fact is that during all that time parliament made only two cuts; $19,000 in supplementary funds for Information Canada in March of 1973, and $1,000 from money intended for the CBC in June of 1973. This illustrates well the manner in which the government has bull-dozed its spending estimates through parliament.
The government has jndulged in questionable advertising campaigns on behalf of government departments reflecting party bias. The taxpayers are paying for the whims of the philosopher king who is engaged in playing games with the election date, thus requiring the CBC to station its technicians and vans on Parliament Hill awaiting the election announcement. This was mentioned last week by one of the previous speakers from our party. The cost estimate given in this regard was a startling figure.
I could go on and list the massive dose of inefficiency this government has given. I have only to mention the fact that the government's deficit today is more than the total budget of the last Conservative government in power by a good many millions of dollars.
For too long the king has thrived under the automatic passage of estimates by May 31. This built-in acceptance mechanism should be removed. Members should be allowed the opportunity to thoroughly examine the estimates before voting on them. That is the only way we can put an end to the spending legacy of this government.
Big Daddy, the biggest spender ever-and that is the federal government-certainly has a great deal to account for in the years to come, and possibly in the forthcoming federal election campaign. The Government of Canada is the greatest spender of all in advertising its own wares, telling the story of how good it is and what it has to offer. This is rather unusual when you consider that the government has no competition. I think of some of the great private concerns which spend millions of dollars to sell their products, such as Procter and Gamble, whose budget for advertising is phenomenal, General Motors, tobacco and alcohol companies. Yet their advertising budgets do not hold a candle to this government's. Certainly if there is a priority for the Comptroller General when he takes office it will be to investigate the advertising campaign in which the present government is involved. There is one particular aspect of one department which requires investigation, and that is the $1 million advertising campaign pointing out abuses to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The Post Office is an important department. I am vitally interested in it as a member of the committee. Some ten years ago this department had a deficit of $67 million. This year the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) says there will be a deficit of approximately $600 million. In 1968, some ten years ago, the employees of the Post Office numbered 36,000. This number has now increased to 66,000, but the service has not improved greatly. It is difficult to know when you can count on a letter being delivered. Let me give an example. Some telegrams were sent to me from my riding of Parry Sound-

Muskoka last Tuesday, some of which were delivered today. Those were telegrams so the House can imagine how much good those telegrams did!
In 1968 there were 236,000 employees of the civil service. Various members of this party have pointed out tonight that the number of employees presently in the civil service is about 500,000. These huges increases should be investigated, and let us hope the Comptroller General will be able to do so.
The proposed budget for this coming year is $45 billion. We are well aware that, with the supplementary estimates which will come in from time to time, by the time March 31 of next year arrives the budget will probably be $50 billion in round figures.
It has already been mentioned that various government departments as well as the government have talked about zero budgeting. However, that is as far as it has gone. Let us hope the Comptroller General will be able to do something to bring these departments to heel, cutting back on overspending.
A suggestion that the Auditor General and the Comptroller General should take into consideration is one involving an incentive system for various departments, having the deputy ministers made responsible. The deputy ministers would have to keep within their budgets or face penalties. If they stayed within the budgets they would receive bonuses. I am aware that deputy ministers are not among the underpaid in this country today, but if they could save taxpayers' money it would be worthwhile giving them an incentive to do so.
I have heard on good authority, and I believe government members will agree, that in certain departments just before March 31 there is an effort to spend that remaining portion of the budget in order that they will receive the same or a greater budget the following year. These people dust around and do their darndest to spend what money is left so that as much or more will be available in the following year. If they could save $300,000 or $400,000 they could be given bonuses of $10,000. I am sure they would think twice then before squandering taxpayers' money. This is an idea the new Comptroller General should consider and perhaps put into practice.
As a member on this side of the House I am in support of this bill. I trust it will accomplish something. Some hon. members are pessimistic about it, but I have the highest praise for the government for bringing it forward even at this late stage. I offer my best wishes to the new Comptroller General. Let him get on with his job as quickly as possible in order that we may stretch taxpayers' dollars a lot further than at the present time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF COMPTROLLER GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed the debate since first reading of this bill with a great deal of interest and attention, especially the views put forward by members of the official opposition. One of the most interesting speeches was made by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), who I am happy to see in the House tonight. That gentleman is the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee. He is the only member of the opposition to hold the
May 1, 1978

position of chairman. Let me say that he carries out his task in this regard in a very excellent fashion. I appreciated the kind words he had for various members of this party, especially for the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) and myself who, along with himself and members from all parties, have had an opportunity of working together in the Public Accounts Committee.
In his speech on this third reading of Bill C-10, he made a very interesting observation, to be found on page 4980 of Hansard dated April 28:
The tireless efforts of the Auditor General through the Standing Committee on Public Accounts have brought a realization that a chief financial officer is indeed needed at the Treasury Board level. Having worked on this subject matter for some time now, I can see the sense of the chief financial officer, the comptroller general, reporting through the Treasury Board to the House, though some of my colleagues may disagree with me. He is the one responsible for putting in place within our agencies, departments and Crown corporations, mechanisms which will demand a better performance in the management of our tax resource.
Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, the great work that was done by the members of the miscellaneous estimates committee to which this bill had been referred. This committee was responsible for calling forth the witnesses to be questioned on this bill regarding the functions and duties of the Comptroller General. On behalf of the minister, I wish to thank all those who have taken part in the debate and the committee hearings in relation to this bill. It was referred to the miscellaneous estimates committee at which time the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), the secretary of the Treasury Board, the Auditor General and the new Comptroller General himself, Mr. Rogers, appeared. We had been told before meeting him that he had been chosen after careful study and was a person who had had a very extensive career in the private * sector in a variety of positions of responsibility with a major international corporation. He indeed impressed all those present with his answers and coolness in spite of the fact it was his first time before a committee of parliament, and there was no doubt that he was an excellent choice.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), who is also in the House tonight, was the only member from the opposition parties who was able to be present throughout the hearings on the day Mr. Rogers appeared as the new Comptroller General replied to questions. Yet everyone who has spoken in this debate keeps saying over and over how important this position of comptroller general is. Further, I hope that in the future more and more members of this House will become more active participants in the Public Accounts Committee. As I know from long experience, this is one of the most important committees in this House.
This is an historic occasion, and as one who has been an active member of the Public Accounts Committee for approximately nine of my 12 years in the House, I join all members in welcoming the official establishment of this new office. I am sure all members will join me in wishing Mr. Rogers well in his new, important duties.
Financial Administration Act
I remind hon. members of the words of the Auditor General in committee when he stated that with this new office and the other changes that have been made since he assumed office, the Canadian government now has the most advanced system of accountability and control of any government in the western world. Even though members may have other priorities and may not become active members of either the Public Accounts Committee or the miscellaneous estimates committee, I would commend to them the reading of the minutes of these committees. Opposition members have especially taken objection to this one-paragraph bill setting up the office of the Comptroller General, but if they study the committee hearings and statements made by the ministers and others they will find the answers to all their questions.
Hon. members will find that in an unresolved conflict existing between the Auditor General and the Comptroller General, if this conflict still exists at the time the Auditor General makes his annual report to parliament, it will be included in that report. This will mean the necessity of a further report to parliament is disproven. In other words, if for some reason Mr. Rogers and Mr. Macdonell cannot come to an agreement on a certain item of government expenditure, then the Auditor General will include it in his report to be tabled in parliament, which is automatically referred to the Public Accounts Committee.
As I previously stated, this committee has been ably chaired by the hon. member for Capilano and other opposition members. Therefore, the committee will be quite free to carry on any investigation it feels necessary. Indeed, neither Mr. Rogers, the Comptroller General, nor the Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell, has any problem with Bill C-10. They are both confident that they can carry out their duties, and have testified to such in committee. I now hope that we can get through third reading of this important bill.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSIST AREAS OF DISPARITY
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSIST AREAS OF DISPARITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) what new initiatives he had in mind to focus more specifically his department's resources in the critical areas of regional disparity, particularly since the department's

budget is down in real terms. Not only is it down in actual cash but new areas have been added and inflation has undermined this department's resources as it has so many other cases.
As it now stands, this department is failing in its task. In 1970, one year after DREE was created, unemployment in Canada stood at 5.7 per cent while in the Atlantic region, a classic area of economic disparity it was 6.2 per cent. Seven years later unemployment in Canada stood at 8.1 per cent while in Atlantic Canada it was 12.7 per cent. Clearly the situation is getting worse instead of better. Economic differences have become more exaggerated and critical.
As the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), our former leader, pointed out a few weeks ago, the result of the combined policies with respect to Canada's various regions is such that to a substantial degree various regions have turned into government dependencies. Energy costs and transportation costs continue to plague the efforts of the Atlantic region to limit its failure to expand as it should.
I want to suggest to the minister tonight that he take steps to educate and work with other departments in order to do something about this lamentable state of affairs. Since the federal government is the largest employer, the largest buyer of goods and services in the country, it is time that the Atlantic region was given more equity.
In 1976, for example, total federal spending on goods and services was about $9.7 billion. Experts and analysts consider that approximately 85 per cent of all procurement is done in central Canada, leaving less than 15 per cent for the other eight provinces and two territories. I remember that shortly after coming to this place the then minister of supply and services stated clearly that his department was going to institute a more enlightened purchasing policy. This has not had any appreciable effect to date.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce also contributes to the under-development of Atlantic Canada. In a recent year, Atlantic Canada received only 1.7 per cent of the funds allotted for industrial assistance. On a per capita basis it should have received over five times as much.
Since my time is very limited tonight, I just want to make a suggestion to the minister. Although both his predecessors had experience in the Department of Transport as well as DREE, by taking the initiative he could accomplish something that they could not, except by paying lip service to the idea, and that is to make transportation a partner with regional economic expansion in attacking disparities in this country.
I should like to suggest this evening that the minister or his parliamentary secretary take a very close look at building something that has been talked about for many years in the Atlantic region, and that is a corridor road extending from the New Brunswick border through northern Maine to the vicinity of Sherbrooke in la belle province, Quebec. A corridor road would be a direct link through the state of Maine from New Brunswick to Quebec. It could be an extension of the Van-ceboro-Lincoln Road at the New Brunswick border which
May 1, 1978

would emerge in the vicinity of Sherbrooke, Quebec after crossing New Brunswick, saving approximately 200 miles on the existing route from Fredericton to Montreal and almost as far by driving through the United States on the existing highway route.
The construction of such a road could perhaps be of more benefit than the St. Lawrence Seaway as far as Atlantic Canada is concerned. It could be and should have been one of the areas of joint co-operation and negotiation between the United States and Canada whenever mutual concessions, aims and objectives were in issue, as for example in the recent pipeline negotiations or when Alaska highway matters are on the table between our two nations.
Such a road would reduce the driving time by approximately four hours and thus allow many additional trips in the course of a year with great savings in energy and maintenance costs. It would bring the Atlantic provinces much closer in real terms to markets in the rest of Canada. Many bulk commodities now tied to rail or water transport could look at potential new markets via road transport. Tourism would be facilitated. There is something to be said for building a road thereby bringing Gagetown, New Brunswick into close linkage with the military installations in the United States. Such a road would be welcome in both countries. It would be expensive. But it would be money well spent compared to some of the cosmetic capital costs involved in building unnecessary and grandiose skyscrapers and monster airports. It would do a great deal in real terms to overcome some of the natural disadvantages geographically that we have in the maritimes.
Let DREE help facilitate the arteries of commerce. We need improvements and opportunities in the maritimes, not handouts. DREE can help but it cannot do much in its present posture. It needs to take steps to either build sound infrastructures and to work with other departments in projects of this magnitude, or make its definition section more flexible. It could allow other industries, except manufacturing and processing industries, to be eligible for DREE aid, as is done in Germany, for example. If we continue to drift along with DREE in its present form, as statistics have shown we are not only perpetuating policies which are not helping the disparate regions of the country, but we are seeing as time goes by a steady erosion of the situation that existed even a few years ago.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ed Lumley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSIST AREAS OF DISPARITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has raised several questions concerning the role of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in Atlantic Canada and in his own province of Nova Scotia with respect to creating employment. While the minister feels that this department's efforts in this regard ought to be well known by now to most Nova Scotians, on the minister's behalf, as his former parliamentary secretary, I am pleased at this time to acquaint the hon. member with what is happening not only in his home province but in his own riding.
Adjournment Debate
He asks what new initiatives the department has in mind. DREE operates in concert with provincial governments in the identification and exploitation of development opportunities. Therefore, I do not unilaterally have new initiatives in mind.
What the department intends to do must also be put in the context of what it is already doing. The department is constantly working, in conjunction with the province, to find new initiatives leading to development agreements. In Nova Scotia the department has signed ten such agreements in less than three years, with a total value approaching one quarter of a billion dollars. We hope in the near future to be announcing further agreements which will contribute in a meaningful and permanent way to the betterment of that province's economy.
The agreements already in force deal with the natural resource sectors, such as forestry, agriculture and minerals. Others deal with industrial development, the Sydney steel mill, the Strait of Canso, tourism and redevelopment of the Halifax-Dartmouth waterfront area.
It is frequently suggested by members of the opposition, that all the department has to do to straighten out our economic problems is to develop our natural resources. We are presently fully committed to the natural resources in Nova Scotia. Another resource, the fisheries, has the full attention of an entire department of the government.
These agreements were not worked out on an ad hoc basis, nor were they proposed as purely political, counter-cyclical measures to create jobs out of thin air. In short, they do not represent the kind of stop-gap measures the hon. member thinks we ought to engage in.
If permanent jobs could be created simply by making interest-free money available to the private sector, we would have recommended this action a long time ago; but this approach is too simplistic. It makes no attempt to recognize the facts of economic life nor, I might add, does it take into account what the availability of too much "free money" would do to our conventional lending institutions.
What we can do, however, and what the department is doing, is to put federal dollars into the economy in such a way that, hopefully, more opportunities for investment will be created. Our development agreements represent the best thinking available as to how to stimulate economic growth by first creating an environment which is attractive to private investment.
This is not easily achieved. Nor can it be done overnight. Broad-based programs for forestry, agriculture, minerals and tourism must by definition be diffuse in their application. They carry with them, however, a number of opportunities for the private sector.
The hon. member might be interested to hear that residents of his own riding and of the surrounding areas have been benefitting from these programs for some time. Grants to farmers in Pictou county during the past two years have

subtopic: FINANCE-MEASURES TO PREVENT DUMPING OF STEEL BEAMS-DEFINITION OF "FAIR WORLD PRICE"
FINANCE-MEASURES TO PREVENT DUMPING OF STEEL BEAMS-DEFINITION OF "FAIR WORLD PRICE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 20 of this year, as reported in Hansard at page 3006, I addressed the following question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The preamble reads:
The heart of much of the regional antagonism caused by federal rulings on matters like the dumping duty on wide-flange steel beams seems to be in our failure to recognize that often more than one market can exist in a country as vast as Canada.
Can the minister, or the Prime Minister, advise whether the government is negotiating an amendment under article 4(A)(ii) of the GATT agreement to reflect the fact that transportation costs and other regional marketing factors may create in Canada two or more markets, where in at least one Canadian producers sell none or almost none of their goods?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) replied as follows:
We have recognized that there is a short-term problem in British Columbia. Of course, when we have one Canadian market we have to maintain a tariff and have an adjudication by the tribunal when it looks into a dumping case- whether it be steel or any other product-because we cannot accept dumping of products on the Canadian market. I am sure the hon. member would not be pleased if we did not protect, in the eastern market, the price of plywood that very often comes from B.C.
In answer to a supplementary question by my hon. friend from Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), the same minister ended his explanation by saying:
Of course, British Columbia producers will always have access to international steel as long as it is not dumped on the Canadian market.
It is not my intention, nor that of the B.C. government, to speak against the principle of protection against dumping. However, for the federal government to continue to treat this vast land with ports on the Atlantic close to European markets and with ports on the Pacific close to Asian and Pacific Rim markets as a single market is to keep in place a policy that is obsolete, a policy that maintains regional stresses, a policy that works against unity and a policy that enhances anti-centralist feeling to the disadvantage of federalism.
My argument against the position taken by the government is that injury should be isolated to the region or market where the injury can be identified. The main factor which determines markets within Canada is railroad freight rates, as anyone who has been in the business of distributing or manufacturing goods knows.
The issue facing us is that tariffs erected to safeguard against injury to domestic producers caused by dumping be considered in two parts; first, within the market regions of Canada where such dumping is causing injury and, second, within market regions of Canada where such dumping is not causing injury. We should limit the safeguard to the region in which the safeguard is prompted as a result of the threat or reality of injury.

As a member of GATT, Canada has accepted the principle of liberalizing trade between member nations. Indeed, this is the thrust of the Tokyo round. The suggested isolation of the safeguard resort would mean protection for the region of Canada needing it, leaving the benefits of freer trade to those not served by domestic production and historically dependent on offshore materials. Surely the federal government can see that this suggestion fits the spirit and objectives of GATT.
To continue as we are today will deliver the West Coast steel fabricating markets to the fabricators of Ontario. The loss to British Columbia will be in neighbourhood of 1,500 to 2,000 jobs, plus all the spin-off benefits attendant to this employment. If the concern of the government for unity and regional equity extends beyond rhetoric, I trust my plea tonight will be given careful consideration by the ministers concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ed Lumley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-MEASURES TO PREVENT DUMPING OF STEEL BEAMS-DEFINITION OF "FAIR WORLD PRICE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) has raised a question concerning the recent move by the government to remit anti-dumping duties on wide flanged steel shapes imported from certain countries for installation in projects in British Columbia, Alberta, Newfoundland and the Yukon Territory. The remission order, as hon. members are aware, will apply for the nine-month period from the application of the provisional anti-dumping duties; that is, for the period from September 29, 1977 to June 29, 1978. As noted in the press announcement, this action was approved to cushion the transition to higher input costs for fabricators in the areas mentioned. As such, it is both limited in coverage and temporary in duration.
The hon. member suggests in his comments that the temporary nature of the remission order will add to the uncertainty facing the steel fabricating industry in British Columbia. Moreover, he is urging that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) act quickly to announce the level of the final dumping duties involved.
Let me first say that it is not the responsibility of the Minister of Finance to determine the level of the anti-dumping duties applicable. The law requires that this decision be taken by the deputy minister of the Department of National Revenue for customs and excise. In this connection I would like to stress, however, that any delay involved in arriving at a final determination should not be attributed to the Department of National Revenue. As I understand the situation, that department has encountered extreme difficulty in obtaining the necessary factual information from the exporters concerned in order to make its findings in such cases. Clearly, much of the uncertainty involved could be eliminated very quickly if the exporters would co-operate with the Department of National Revenue to this end.
With regard to the temporary nature of the remission order, I can assure the hon. member that the matter was given very careful consideration by the government prior to taking a decision. In this instance the government was faced with a

request from the provinces of British Columbia and Newfoundland to assist their fabricating industries to adjust to a new situation. This new situation resulted directly from a decision by the anti-dumping tribunal that dumped imports of the steel product in question were causing injury to domestic production. This decision, by a court of record, was in full conformity with the terms of the Anti-Dumping Act passed by this parliament. The government, in light of the representations it received, felt that a limited remission was warranted in this instance to enable time for the regional fabricating industry to adjust.
It must, however, be clearly recognized that the real issue at stake here is whether Canada is prepared to allow its domestic industry to suffer injury by unfair trading practices of other countries. The government has in the past and will in the future use all the means at its disposal to provide the environment in which our domestic producers can be assured of fair trading practices. At this particular time the steel industry worldwide is facing difficulty. This is expected to continue until such time as the world economy picks up. Other governments have taken special measures to guard against predatory dumping of steel into their markets. The Department of National Revenue has also stepped up its activity to ensure that steel is not injuriously dumped into the Canadian market in massive quantities.
