speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-COST-SHARING OF TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 3 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question about cost-sharing and the reconstruction and improvement of the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland. I asked him would his government agree to a cost-sharing arrangement of 75 per cent federal and 25 per cent provincial, as the province had asked. The province originally asked for a 90-10 deal. The Prime Minister said that I should ask the DREE minister. He thought it was a matter for DREE. Mr. Speaker, this shows you how little the Prime Minister knows about what is going on in his government.
Negotiations were going on with the department of transportation, the minister of transportation of the Newfoundland government, since May of 1973 at least, over this cost-sharing arrangement. The Prime Minister is governing in the dark. The left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. He is pirouetting in the deep purple. Either that or he is so dithered about the election and whether to call it or not, or he is so puzzled about patronage, that he does not know what is happening in his own government.
In 1965 the trans-Canada highway, Mr. Speaker, was completed under the great slogan "We'll finish the drive in '65 thanks to Mr. Pearson". That is when the federal government agreed to pay 90 per cent of the cost of completing the
Adjournment Debate
trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland. But the highway was build to substandard; it was not built to the trans-Canada standards on the mainland. It was substandard then, and since then, Mr. Speaker, federal neglect of their obligations with respect to the Newfoundland railway and CNR neglect of the needs of the Newfoundland railway and mismanagement of the Newfoundland railway has resulted in most freight now being taken by truck rather than by rail cars across Newfoundland.
The figures are staggering. In the year 1971, 2,500 tractor trailers landed at Port aux Basques to go across the Island. In 1976, 28,000, a huge increase in traffic. In 1970 the railway moved 385,000 tons of freight. In 1976, six years later, just 397,000 tons, only a 3 per cent increase. But whereas in 1970 there were 3,292 truck and trailer units operating in Newfoundland, it went to 17,247 in 1976, a 424 per cent increase. In 1976, trucks carried about 90 per cent of all the freight carried across Newfoundland.
In addition, the federal government and CNR conspired with Mr. Smallwood, when he was premier of Newfoundland, to do away with the railway passenger service in that province, and since 1968 we have had a bus service only for passengers travelling across Newfoundland. The result is there is this tremendous increase in traffic on the substandard trans-Canada highway.
The highway is deteriorating completely. Anyone who trucks on that highway will tell you, as did the St. John's Board of Trade a few months ago, that repairs to transport equipment skyrocketed; the transport trucks are damaged by the condition of the highway. They said also:
And claims by business to the truckers have doubled because the freight being hauled across this province "has literally been smashed to pieces".
Of course, those costs are being met by the consumer. This is happening in a province like Newfoundland with its weak financial condition, with the federal government letting CN concur in the dumping of all the freight on the small and narrow Trans-Canada Highway, and with our recognition that
we are a special case, as was found by the MacPherson Royal Commission which stated in 1962:
The situation in Newfoundland is a special case distinct from the rest of Canada.
You cannot put it any plainer than that. They are finding that a highway network is beyond our resources and the government should see that the provincial government has money for roads other than the trans-Canada. At least a 90-10 deal is needed for the next ten years in the reconstruction of the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland and its strengthening and upgrading. The province simply cannot find 50 per cent of the $250 million required.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), with his Teutonic, terrorist transport tactics, sent wires to the four Atlantic premiers in June of this year telling them that they would cost share 50-50 only, and that if they did not accept this 50-50 offer, the money would be used for some other purpose by the federal government. Because of this ultimatum, they all col-

lapsed, with Newfoundland falling in line on March 29 of this year. Newfoundland surrendered and accepted this pitiful and incomplete offer. So instead of "We'll finish the drive in 65, thanks to Mr. Pearson", what we have now is: "On the Newfoundland highway, you drive with a bang, until you get rid of Otto Lang". We must get some minister of transport in there that is not hip on the user-pay principle of the present minister and who will treat Newfoundland fairly in this direction.
The present transport policy is to discontinue ferry subsidies in Newfoundland; it is to put an inadequate search and rescue service there; it is not to give us any kind of ice breaking service at all; it is to continue withdrawals by CN Marine and the CNR and an inferior ferry service from the mainland to Argentia.
This Minister of Transport will languish in history as the least sympathetic, the least useful, the most loutish and the most lumpish of all federal ministers of transport ever seen. His actions in Newfoundland, to put the best face on it, are barbaric. I am asking the government now to change this unilateral decision of theirs that they will finance only 50 per cent of the cost. We are talking of $250 million over ten years, not $250 million that must be spent this year, next year or the year after. It will cost $250 million over ten years, of which the federal government is now offering $125 million if they go for the whole ten years. This is a three-year agreement only. It should be a 75 per cent deal at least.
If you look at the brief submitted by the Canadian Railway Labour Association to the Government of Canada on March 20 of this year you will see what happened in Newfoundland. It reads:
In sum, what we now have on the island of Newfoundland is an inefficient passenger service; an inefficient freight service; a fast deteriorating trans-Canada highway and a rail system, operated by the frustrated Crown corporation, the Canadian National Railways; a federal transport policy based upon "commercial viability" and "user-pay concept".
That is what we have now in Newfoundland. What is to be done? If this government will not do it, then the next government, which will be of a different political persuasion-we hope, in any event-will have to do it, and that is to give the province of Newfoundland better financial terms to put across the island a decent trans-Canada highway and ensure that the Newfoundland railway continues to operate more efficiently and at a more reasonable freight rate, so that much of this freight traffic will go off the highway and back on to the Newfoundland railway where it belongs.
So I call upon the Minister of Transport, in his last month of office, to stop this loutish behaviour and to give Newfoundland a fair deal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-COST-SHARING OF TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really do not see where the hon. member is getting at with all the wordiness and verbal inflation that he uses when speaking of the Minister of Transport and even of the right hon. Prime Minister, who have spent all their energy in harmonizing the policies of the Departments of Regional Economic Expansion, Transport, and others in consultation with the provinces, in order to give the Maritimes the best possible road system for the best possible service to the population of those provinces.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to confirm that on Tuesday, April 18, the Minister of Transport of Canada and the minister of transportation and communication of Newfoundland signed an official agreement regarding a three year road improvement program for Newfoundland. This program will involve expenditures of almost $60 million. The agreement concludes fruitful negotiations with the four Atlantic provinces, and the road improvement program can thus be implemented without delay.
As the hon. member of the opposition is aware, the federal government agreed, in May 1977, to spend up to $125 million over the next three years to upgrade the transport system in the Maritimes, and a large proportion of that amount, namely $100 million, is earmarked for the highway improvement program, which is a program whose costs are shared equally by the provinces and the Government of Canada.

Work to be undertaken over the next three years in Newfoundland includes construction of additional lanes at selected locations between St. John's and Highway 70; strengthening and upgrading between highways 201 and 210; also between Port Blandford and Terra Nova Park, and between the park and Highway 320; between Georges Lake and Crabbes River; and between Bishop's Falls and Grand Falls. In addition, the agreement provides for the standardization of allowable axle weights and gross vehicle weights for truck using the primary highway systems.
In closing, I should emphasize that the government is anxiously awaiting recommendations from the Sullivan commission, which is reviewing transportation on Newfoundland. Of course, this recently signed agreement will not affect any of the recommendations which may arise from the commission's findings.
